strengths: Comprehensive theoretical framework systematically analyzing RLHF vs. DPO across four model mis-specification conditions, providing structured understanding of when each method outperforms
Novel insight that online DPO can outperform both RLHF and standard DPO under isomorphic mis-specified model classes (Proposition 7), which is counterintuitive
Concrete sample complexity separation showing RLHF achieves O(k log d/n) vs. DPO's Ω(d/n) in dual-token sparse prediction task, with both ℓ₀ and ℓ₁-regularized analyses
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation, comprehensive appendices, and empirical validation on controlled experiments aligned with theoretical predictions
Theoretical results validated through both controlled experiments and connection to large-scale empirical studies (Razin et al., Swamy et al., Xu et al., etc.)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: relies heavily on standard tools (performance difference lemmas, sparse recovery results from Yao et al. [2025]); authors acknowledge using 'relatively simple techniques'

Significant gap between theory and practice: restrictive linear parameterization assumptions, exact optimization setting (infinite data), small-scale experiments on GPT-2-Large (774M), single dataset (PKU-SafeRLHF)

Statistical separation result (Theorem 10) is task-specific to DTSP; double-token construction appears artificially designed to create separation; generalizability to natural preference learning unclear

Incomplete practical guidance: Conditions 6-7 for unequal model classes state 'either method may outperform depending on environment' without actionable criteria; no method to determine model class relationships for real models

Partial relaxation of realizability: still requires specific model class relationships (Conditions 1-7) rather than general mis-specification; no characterization of how often each condition occurs in practice
Theorem 2 (online DPO): requires δ-bounded error and PILAF sampler; tightness of δ constraint and behavior for δ = Ω(R_max) not analyzed; results rely on specific numerical constructions

Experimental limitations: only one dataset tested, 'exact optimization' uses empirical not ground-truth rewards, limited to small models, no ablation studies or comparisons with other methods (IPO only mentioned in appendix)

strengths: Systematic theoretical framework removing realizability assumption and studying comprehensive model misspecification scenarios (Conditions 1-7), advancing beyond prior work

Novel statistical efficiency separation (Theorem 10) showing DPO requires Ω(d/n) samples while RLHF achieves Õ(√k log d/n) for sparse rewards, with insightful explanation about value function distortion
Clear characterization of dichotomy when each method is superior (Table 1) with concrete propositions for different misspecification regimes
Valuable observation about token-level parameterization showing DPO must learn more complex q* function entangled with base model, providing insight into why policy model may need larger scale
Strong connection to practice through Section 5.2 showing theoretical predictions validated by recent large-scale empirical studies (Razin et al., Swamy et al., Xu et al.)
Technically rigorous proofs with comprehensive appendix; shows PILAF sampler cannot close gap under policy misspecification (Proposition 4), challenging existing literature
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, Table 1 summary, and honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Limited practical validation: small-scale experiments (GPT-2-LARGE-774M only) on single dataset (PKU-SafeRLHF) with no large-scale benchmark evaluation; results on controlled settings don't validate scalability to modern LLMs

Finite-sample analysis (Section 4) restricted to artificially constructed Dual-Token Sparse Prediction task with engineered feature structure ψ(a,b) = ψ(b) + (r_dense^T ψ(a))e_1; authors acknowledge inability to extend to 3+ tokens for mathematical reasons, limiting generality

Restrictive and somewhat artificial assumptions: Assumption 13 requires specific preference data construction; well-conditioned spectrum assumption (λ_min = λ_max = Θ(1/d)) may not hold generally; lower bounds require engineered vocabulary with three token groups
Limited practical guidance: unclear which method practitioners should choose in realistic scenarios with partial misspecification and finite samples; no guidance on practical model scale decisions

Gap between theory and practice: token-level linear parameterization analysis may not capture nonlinear transformer behavior; exact optimization analysis (Section 3) less practically relevant than finite-sample regime
Incremental improvements over concurrent work: Section 3 extends Swamy et al. (2026) with similar structure; comparison to Nika et al. (2024) shows improvements but updates are somewhat incremental
Missing analyses: no computational efficiency comparison, no online learning dynamics, no sensitivity to hyperparameter β, limited exploration of coverage conditions
